articleTitle: Genetically derived filter circuits using preferred value components
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: In the realisation of discrete-component analogue electronic circuits it is common practice, because of costs, to specify passive component values from a set preferred of values. For the design of integrated circuits it can also be desirable to use a standard set of passive component values. For example, to obtain accurate ratio matching of integrated resistors and capacitors by stacking identical unit valued components. The usual design approaches produce circuits in which the permitted component values are assumed to be unrestricted. The circuit is then converted to a practical circuit by simple rounding of the exact component values to the nearest value in the permitted set. Of course, in general the circuit performance realised will differ from the ideal. It may then be necessary to repeat the design with a more stringent specification or to use a more closely spaced set of permitted values, both of which can have cost implications. However if other combinations of permitted values are considered, a better circuit performance may potentially be achieved than that obtained by simple rounding. The difficulty is that in all but trivially simple circuits the space of all feasible combinations to be searched is huge. Genetic algorithms (GAs) can be used to search this space. There the application is to a simple second order active filter specified by its transfer function parameters. The aim of the present contribution is to show that GAs can be successfully applied to more complex filter structures. Moreover the optimal search is carried out directly on the frequency-response template specification rather than on a specified approximating ideal transfer function, thereby avoiding this additional source of approximation. The next section outlines the basic GA and its implementation for the present application. Results are then given for practical filter examples. An all-pole low pass response is considered with template specified by a 1 dB pass band ripple with a pass band edge at 10/sup 5/ rad/sec, and stop band attenuation of -150 dB at a stop band edge of 10/sup 6/ rad/sec. The GA is used to generate both LC ladder structures and the more complex FDNR active RC structures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CMOS +1V to -1V, rail to rail operational amplifier
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: A fully differential operational amplifier operating within a 2 V power supply range is presented. The amplifier was designed using 1.2 mu m CMOS technology and uses multi-regulation techniques to provide a high open loop gain magnitude without degrading the open loop phase response. In order to overcome the limited input common mode voltage range due to the low power supply rails, fully differential complementary techniques are employed. The output voltage swing extends to be within 0.2 V of the lower and upper power supply rails.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A review of dual current-feedback amplifier techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: Current feedback amplifiers (CFAs) offer excellent performance, especially in terms of slew-rate and bandwidth, and are now widely used particularly for video signal processing. However, some of the parameters of CFAs, such as CMRR, are disappointingly poor. Also, the topology, which is markedly different from the classical voltage feedback op-amp (VFA), means that the CFA cannot directly replace the VFA in a number of important application circuits, most notably the simple single amplifier Miller integrator. Monolithic dual CFAs can be configured to overcome some of the disadvantages of using a single CFA device, with net performance improvements and versatility approaching that of the VFA. In this paper some dual CFA amplifier techniques are reviewed and a clear insight into the operation and advantages is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: The analogue noise control system described reduces a pulse radar system thermal noise floor variation (due to variability between units and temperature) from about 10 dB down to 4 dB. It also enhances the effect of the post detector logarithmic amplifier particularly in its highest gain state leading to an improvement in the ability to visually detect displayed targets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New small-signal macromodel for current-feedback op-amps
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: Current feedback operational amplifiers (CFOA) are now recognised for their excellent performance in high speed and high slew-rate analog signal processing applications. Simple circuit level macromodels of the conventional voltage op-amp (VOA) are useful in analysis and give the applications engineer valuable insight into the operation of the VOA, and the same is true for the CFOA. Semiconductor manufacturers' macromodels for the CFOA enable application circuit performance predictions to be made rapidly, but they are generally too complex to provide insight into the operation of the device. The almost universal 'standard' CFOA simple circuit level small-signal macromodel does enable closed-loop gain predictions to be made. However, it is over simplified and cannot be used to predict closed-loop input and output impedance levels with any accuracy, nor the effects of load impedance on the performance of the CFOA. In this paper a new simplified small-signal macromodel is introduced which models the input and output common-collector buffer stages of the CFOA as a composite BJT and is shown to give improved insight into the small-signal operation of the CFOA.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Tunable current mirror technique for high frequency analog design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: In this paper, we propose a very simple but powerful method of bandwidth enhancement for general CMOS current-mirror circuits. Introducing a compensation resistor between the gates of the primary transistor pair of the current-mirror can lead to a significant bandwidth enhancement.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A SPICE macromodel for operational transconductance amplifiers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: Operational transconductance amplifiers (OTAs) are now being used in the realization of continuous time active filters. The OTA can be used to simulate inductors and lossy integrators for ladder filter realizations or to realise grounded capacitor canonical structures of arbitrary transfer functions. Commercial applications include filters for HDTV operating at frequencies up to 20 MHz using MOS technology. Modern design techniques place heavy emphasis on circuit simulation to reduce hardware prototyping costs. Analogue systems based upon the operational amplifier (op-amp) as the active element have used macro models for many years. Macro models are used because they simulate the terminal characteristics of an op-amp with linear elements, rather than modelling the computationally intensive non-linear behaviour of a number of large transistor based circuits. Macro model based simulations are thus faster than non-linear simulations of an op-amp design saving design time and reducing development costs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: A new class of micropower analogue filter is proposed. We present a section of a second-order continuous time filter employing MOSFETs operating in weak inversion. The idea is based upon the recently proposed log-domain filter approach used previously in bipolar technology. Simulation result using SPICE and applications are also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High accuracy and high speed current-conveyor
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: Current processing building-blocks provide wide bandwidth and high speed, but are often open-loop and as such not very accurate. A typical circuit is the current-conveyor, in which the low accuracies in both voltage and current transfer functions have limited its acceptability. In order to increase the circuit accuracy and speed simultaneously, a new design approach has been adopted and a high speed and high accuracy current-conveyor has been obtained. By using a complementary bipolar process based on the XFCB parameters from Analog Devices Inc, simulation shows that the voltage transfer function exhibits a 2.67 GHz-3 dB bandwidth with improved unity gain accuracy. Also very high slew-rate is obtained, which can reach 6000 V/ mu s and the settling time to 0.1% is within 15 ns.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improved charge pump phase detector for digital phase-locked loop
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Analogue Signal Processing
abstract: The impact of dead band in charge pump phase detectors on the performance of DPLLs (Digital Phase-Locked Loops) has been well reported for a number of years. It is widely accepted that the standard form of charge pump phase detector tends to suffer from an inability to track small phase perturbations at its input. This tends to arise from the technology employed, which is generally MOS based, since it lends itself to both low cost and low power implementation. Consequently, techniques have to-be employed which remove the nonlinear gain region such that during the zero phase error condition the current sources are switched on for a finite period of time (thus removing the dead band condition). A drawback with this technique is that an increased noise current is injected into the loop, and consequently, the phase noise close-to-carrier may degrade. The purpose of this paper is to discuss in detail the imperfections which arise in charge pump phase detectors, analysing both spurious and phase noise mechanisms. This leads to an improved charge pump arrangement which provides both improved sideband suppression and phase noise performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
